Let \(n\) be a positive integer. We prove the result with \(c=\frac27\) and \(d=5\).

For the lower bound, consider any terminal configuration using \(m\) blocks. For \(n\ge2\), there are \(n(n-2)\) horizontal and \(n(n-2)\) vertical triples, hence \(2n(n-2)\) potential triples. Terminality implies that every potential triple contains a removed stamp.

A horizontal removed block intersects at most five horizontal triples, since the starting position of an intersecting triple has at most five possibilities. Each of its three stamps belongs to at most three vertical triples, so it intersects at most nine vertical triples. Thus it intersects at most fourteen potential triples. The same bound holds for a vertical removed block. Therefore
\[
14m\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
and hence
\[
m\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
This holds for every terminal configuration, so
\[
b(n)\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
For \(n=1\), the inequality is immediate.

For the upper bound, index the infinite square grid by integer pairs. In row \(i\), place horizontal blocks whose starting columns are all integers congruent to \(i\pmod 5\). Thus the marked positions are exactly those \((i,j)\) satisfying
\[
j-i\pmod5\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
These blocks are pairwise disjoint.

Every horizontal triple meets the marked set because, in a fixed row, only two consecutive residue classes modulo five are unmarked. Every vertical triple also meets it. Indeed, for the triple in column \(j\) and rows \(r,r+1,r+2\), writing \(x=j-r\), its three positions are marked respectively when
\[
x\in\{0,1,2\},\qquad x\in\{1,2,3\},\qquad x\in\{2,3,4\}\pmod5.
\]
These sets cover all residues modulo five.

Now tear out every periodic block lying wholly inside the \(n\times n\) board. Each row contains at most \(n/5+1\) such blocks, so their number is at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n.
\]
Let \(B\) be the set of stamps in the first two or last two columns; then \(|B|\le4n\). Any triple remaining after the initial removals must meet \(B\): it meets some marked position in the infinite pattern, and the periodic block containing that position was omitted only because it crossed the left or right boundary. Every position of such a block that lies on the board belongs to \(B\).

Continue greedily removing available triples until none remains. Any triple available at a later stage was also available immediately after the initial removals, since removals can only destroy triples. Hence every additional block meets \(B\). The additional blocks are disjoint, so they use distinct stamps of \(B\); consequently there are at most \(4n\) additional blocks.

Thus a terminal configuration exists using at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n+4n=\frac15n^2+5n
\]
blocks. Therefore
\[
b(n)\le \frac15n^2+5n.
\]
Combining the bounds gives, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac17n^2-\frac27n\le b(n)\le\frac15n^2+5n.
\]
Hence the required constants may be chosen as \(c=\frac27\) and \(d=5\).
input.theorem:
I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).
